transcript.text: I manage a small retention team at a subscription company. We can phone only 50 customers a month, out of about 1,200. I want to know which 50 to call. The table I shared has one row per customer: signup date, segment, city, plan, tenure, monthly spend, support tickets in the last 90 days, and whether they churned the next month. A call costs us about the same for every customer; a customer who stays is worth their monthly spend. We do not know yet whether a call changes anyone's mind. [shares customers.csv]

I understood your situation: your retention team can phone 50 of about 1,200 customers each month, and you want the call list where each call is most likely to save a customer worth their monthly spend. The table (customers.csv, 1,200 rows) has one row per customer — signup date, segment, city, plan, tenure, monthly spend, recent support tickets, and whether they churned the next month. Calls cost the same per customer, and you don't yet know whether a call changes anyone's mind.

Here's the real problem: ranking customers by churn risk is only half the job. The value of calling someone depends on whether they'd have stayed anyway *and* whether a call can change their mind — and that second part is unknown. So my approach is to offer three paths that handle that unknown differently:

1. **Prediction first** — train a churn-risk model on the table, score all 1,200 customers, rank by predicted risk × monthly spend, and call the top 50 each month.
2. **Experiment first** — run a randomized pilot: call 50 random customers, hold out a matched 50 not called, and compare next-month churn to learn whether calls work at all before you target.
3. **Simple ranking now** — rank by the risk signals already visible (support tickets, tenure, plan, segment) × monthly spend, no model, immediate call list.

The plan, whichever you pick:

1. You choose an option; I check it against your table and confirm what gets built.
2. Build or run it: model training and scoring, or the pilot split, or the table ranking — producing your first top-50 call list.
3. You call the 50, record who was called, and measure next-month churn among called vs. not-called customers.
4. Review whether calls moved the number; re-score or re-run monthly, and stop or expand once the effect is clear enough to trust.

Since we don't know whether calls work, I'd lean toward Option 2 (experiment first) so your targeting rests on evidence rather than assumption — or pairing a pilot with Option 1 so you learn while you target.

Which direction would you like to take — or would you rather I decide for you?

choices.title: Option 1 — Prediction first: rank by churn risk × monthly spend
choices.what: Train a model on customers.csv to predict next-month churn from signup date, segment, city, plan, tenure, monthly spend, and recent support tickets. Score all 1,200 customers, rank by predicted churn probability × monthly spend (expected value of saving them), and call the top 50 each month. You get: A churn-risk score for every customer, a ranked top-50 call list each month, and model performance metrics so you can see how well the score separates leavers from stayers. Trade-off: It assumes the customers most likely to churn are the ones a call can save — that's unproven, and the model cannot tell you whether calls work at all. Effort: Moderate: one model build, then a monthly re-score and call list.

choices.title: Option 2 — Experiment first: test whether calls change anyone's mind
choices.what: Run a small randomized pilot: call 50 customers chosen at random, hold out a matched group of 50 who are not called, and compare next-month churn between the two groups (and across segments). That gives a direct answer to whether a call changes anyone's mind and how much it is worth per segment before you spend all 50 calls on targeting. You get: An evidence-based answer to whether calls work at all, an estimated effect size per segment, and a go/no-go on whether targeting is worth doing. Trade-off: This month's calls fund learning rather than guaranteed saves, and you need a few months of pilot results to trust the effect. Effort: Low: defining the random split and measuring outcomes; no model training.

choices.title: Option 3 — Simple ranking now: no model, just the signals you already see
choices.what: Rank customers using the risk signals already in the table — recent support tickets, short tenure, plan, segment — combined with monthly spend, and call the top 50 without training anything. You get: An immediate top-50 call list this month, fast and transparent, with no model to maintain. Trade-off: Less precise than a model, and it still rests on the unproven idea that high-risk customers are the most savable. Effort: Minutes: a few aggregate queries over the table.
